# FluidNC Motion Setup

Follow this process to setup and debug motion on a new FluidNC machine.

> Before you start to test the motion be sure your startup messages are free of all errors and warnings. See the [troubleshooting guide](http://wiki.fluidnc.com/en/support/troubleshooting_config_files) for help with that.
{.is-warning}


## Motion Flow Chart

Click on a box for more information.  You can also use the side navigation bar to go to the sections.

```diagram

```


## Initial Setup
* Set [idle_ms](/config/axes#idle_ms) to 255 so steppers stay enabled. (Later, after everything is working, you can set idle_ms to a different value so the motors are not always enabled, if that is appropriate for your machine.)
* Start with slow [acceleration_mm_per_sec2](/config/axes#acceleration_mm_per_sec2) values, for example 20
* Start with slow [max_rate_mm_per_min](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) values, for example 1000
* Using [WebInstaller](https://installer.fluidnc.com/) Terminal or FluidTerm, send **G91 G0** to enable incremental mode, so you can easily move in either direction.

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)

## Try to Move an Axis
* After setup as above, you can send motion commands like:
* **X10**   to move the X axis forward by 10 mm
* **X-10** to move the X axis backward by 10 mm
* **Y10** to move the Y axis forward by 10 mm
* etc

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)

## Debug No Motion
```diagram

```


[Top](#motion-flow-chart)

### Motor Lock
When a stepper motor is powered, it will be difficult or impossible to turn by hand.  This is called “motor lock”.  Conversely, if the motor is unpowered - either as a result of the driver not having power or the driver’s enable signal in inactive - it is usually fairly easy to manually rotate the motor shaft.
When a motor goes from the unlocked to locked state, you can often hear a “thunk” sound.  A locked stepper motor will also usually be warm to the touch.
For an external stepper driver, the “enable” signal is usually actually a “disable”.  If you do not connect anything to the ENA input of an external stepper driver, the motor will lock.


[Back](#debug-no-motion)

### Debug Motor Not Locked
If a motor is not locked, there are several possibilities
*  [idle_ms](/config/axes#idle_ms) is not set to 255 (see [Initial Setup](#Initial_Setup))
* The stepper driver has no power
* The wiring from the stepper driver to the motor is bad
* The motor is bad - both windings are burned out and will read infinite resistance on an ohmmeter
* The enable / disable signal to the stepper driver is in the “disabled” state
* The disable wiring could be bad (but for external drivers, unconnected wires means “enable”)
* The [disable_pin](/config/axes#disable_pin): setting in the yaml config file could have the wrong polarity.
* Some external drivers have a 5V/24V switch that must be set to 5V in order to enable it to work with the 5V signals coming from a FluidNC controller.

> Be sure to test the lock by trying to rotate the motors in the lock AND unlock states. Ignore the text responses from FluidNC. That is just showing you what FluidNC is trying to do. Also, some motors under load will "thunk" for both lock and unlock transitions, so do not use that to determine the lock state. 
{.is-info}

### Stepper Enable/Disable
If you have external stepper drivers and their ENA input is not connected, the steppers should lock whenever power is applied to the drivers.  Some external drivers have a “charge pump” safety feature that can be disabled with a switch.  If so, you should disable that feature.
Stepstick driver modules and onboard driver chips usually have an enable line that FluidNC can control.  Some controllers have one such line that disables all of the drivers as a group - see [shared_stepper_disable_pin](/config/axes#shared_stepper_disable_pin).  Other controllers have separate lines so each driver can be controlled individually - see [disable_pin](/config/axes#disable_pin) .  In typical use, FluidNC will automatically enable the drivers before starting any motion, and then after motion has stopped for a configurable amount of time - see [idle_ms](/config/axes#idle_ms) - they will be disabled.  If [idle_ms](/config/axes#idle_ms) is 255, FluidNC will leave them enabled all the time unless you use [\$MD](/features/commands_and_settings#motordisable-or-md) to disable them manually.
You can manually disable the drivers by sending or manually enable with [\$ME](/features/commands_and_settings#motorenable-or-me).  If [$MD](/features/commands_and_settings#motordisable-or-md) enables and [\$ME](/features/commands_and_settings#motorenable-or-me) disables, the polarity of the corresponding enable line is wrong.

[Back](#debug-no-motion)

### Motor Clicking or Buzzing
If a stepper motor makes clicking sounds instead of moving, the usual cause is that it is trying to go too fast.  Possible causes include:
* [acceleration_mm_per_sec2](/config/axes#acceleration_mm_per_sec2) is too high.  That is like stalling an engine by stomping on the accelerator.  The stepper motor will stall out before it gets up to speed
* [max_rate_mm_per_min](/config/axes#max_rate_mm_per_min) is too high.  The motor will start moving then stall when it gets up to a certain speed.
* Driver current is misconfigured at too low a value for the motors.
* Bad wiring between the driver and the motor

[Back](#debug-no-motion)

### Motor Won't Move
If a stepper motor locks but silently will not move, it is usually because the step signal (sometimes labeled PUL for pulse) is not getting to the driver
* [step_pin](/config/axes#step_pin) could have the wrong value
* [pulse_us](/config/axes#pulse_us) could be too low.  This is rarely a problem for onboard or stepstick drivers, but can be a problem with external drivers, especially older ones that use TB6560 modules
* Bad wiring to the PUL input of an external driver
* PUL and DIR are swapped

See [Testing Step Pins](/support/setup/testing-step-pins) for one way to test Step and Direction pins.

[Back](#debug-no-motion)

## Swap Axes
If, say, you asked to move X but Y moved instead, you must swap the X and Y axes

Option 1 - Swap the X and Y motor cables

Option 2 - In the yaml config file, replace the “x:” label with “y:”, and vice versa

Option 3 - In the yaml config file, swap the [step_pin](/config/axes#step_pin):, [direction_pin](/config/axes#direction_pin):, and possibly the [disable_pin](/config/axes#disable_pin): values between the x: and y: sections.

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)
## Swap Direction
Option 1 - Swap a pair of wires in the stepper cable - [like this](https://www.reddit.com/r/ender3/comments/s6fv2x/switching_stepper_motor_direction_steppers_in/)

Option 2 - In the yaml config file, find the [direction_pin](/config/axes#direction_pin): for the axis that is going backwards.  Either add or remove :low from the value.  For example, if it says **direction_pin: gpio.12**, change that to **direction_pin: gpio.12:low**.  Conversely, if it already says **gpio.12:low**, change it to **gpio.12**.

Reference

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)
## Debug One Direction
If the axis will only move in one direction, the most common reason is a problem with the direction signal to the stepper driver.  Possibilities include:
* Bad wiring of the direction signal to an external driver
* Incorrect value for [direction_pin](/config/axes#direction_pin) 

### Erratic Direction
Another possibility is a bad connection between the stepper driver and the motor, so that only one of the two motor coils is getting power.  The most common manifestation of this problem is that the direction is erratic, randomly switching directions, but that can sometimes be mistaken as one-direction-only. 

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)
## Adjust steps_per_mm
The amount that the axis moves for each pulse that is sent to the stepper motor driver is controlled by [steps_per_mm](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) .  It is affected by the mechanical system (screw pitch, pulley sizes, etc) and by the driver’s “microstepping” setting.  If you understand how all this works, you can calculate the correct value for [steps_per_mm](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) .  Otherwise, you can just change [steps_per_mm](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) until it works.  If you asked to move 10 mm but it actually moved 5 mm, you would need to double the [steps_per_mm](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) value.  In general, multiply [steps_per_mm](/config/axes#steps_per_mm) by the factor expected_distance / actual_distance .

[Back](#motion-flow-chart)
## Adjust Speed

Once an axis is moving reliably, going the specified distance and direction, you can adjust [acceleration_mm_per_sec2](/config/axes#acceleration_mm_per_sec2) and [max_rate_mm_per_min](/config/axes#max_rate_mm_per_min) to make it go faster.  One convenient test procedure is to set [max_rate_mm_per_min](/config/axes#max_rate_mm_per_min) to a very high value then use **G1 Fnnn** moves to test at specific rates, then when you have settled on a good top end rate, set [max_rate_mm_per_min](/config/axes#max_rate_mm_per_min) to that limiting value.
When acceleration is low, the machine might not reach the top speed before half of the distance, so it will then switch to deceleration without ever “cruising”.  Use long distances and bump up the acceleration until the motors stall near the beginning of the acceleration phase.  Then back off the acceleration so it doesn't stall and start increasing the rate.
When you have discovered how fast your machine can travel, test with loads, especially for machines with spindles that can experience side loads.  You will want to decrease the max rate so that it will not stall under any reasonable situation.  Keep in mind that, over time, things get worse due to lubrication conditions, wear, debris, temperature, etc.  Give yourself some headroom by using conservative settings.
